subject: chemistry
subtopic: Introduction to the particulate nature of matter
title: Separating a gas mixture without changing its particles
stem: The sealed vessel contains the particles shown. Filled atoms are X and open atoms are Y. A selective membrane passes only X₂ particles; it does not split any particle. Every drawn particle represents the same number of real particles. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the elemental substances and compound, and calculate the X: Y atom ratio in the original vessel.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: All X₂ passes through the membrane. Find the fraction of original particles remaining and the fraction of remaining particles that are XY₂.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why this process is a physical separation and why it cannot produce a sample containing only separate X atoms.

steps.text: X₂ and Y₂ are elements; XY₂ is a compound.
Count 2 X₂, 3 Y₂ and 4 XY₂: X atoms = 8, Y atoms = 14.
There were 9 particles and 7 remain.
Remaining fraction 7/9; XY₂ fraction among those remaining 4/7.
No bonds within X₂, Y₂ or XY₂ have been broken or formed.
The membrane selects intact particles by a physical property.
Obtaining separate X atoms from these substances would require breaking covalent bonds, which this process does not do.

title: Interpreting two plateaus on a heating curve
stem: A pure substance is heated at constant power. The schematic curve has melting plateau B–C lasting 4.0 min at 0.0 °C and boiling plateau D–E lasting 12.0 min at 100.0 °C. No energy is lost. For a fixed sample, supplied energy equals power × time. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State the phases present on each plateau and explain why temperature remains constant although energy is supplied.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Compare the energy supplied during vaporization with that during melting.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Compare the average kinetic energies at the two plateaus. Explain why 100/0 is not a valid calculation.

steps.text: B–C: solid and liquid; D–E: liquid and gas.
Energy changes intermolecular separation/arrangement rather than increasing mean particle kinetic energy.
Temperature, which measures average kinetic energy on the kelvin scale, therefore remains constant during each phase change.
Constant power makes energy proportional to plateau duration.
Vaporization energy is 12.0/4.0 = 3.0 times melting energy.
Use absolute temperatures 273.15 K and 373.15 K.
Ratio = 373.15/273.15 = 1.37 to 3 significant figures.
Celsius zero is not zero kinetic energy; only absolute temperature has the required proportionality.

subject: chemistry
title: An isotope collection and its charged particles
stem: The drawing is a counted collection of ten silicon atoms, not a mass spectrum: eight have 14 neutrons, one has 15, and one has 16. Every atom has atomic number 14. Treat isotope masses as their integer mass numbers. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write the three isotope symbols and find the mean relative atomic mass of this collection.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: One atom of the heaviest isotope forms Si²⁺. State its proton, neutron and electron counts and explain which counts change.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A second ten-atom collection has the same total number of protons but a larger mass. Explain whether it must have the same isotope abundances and whether its ordinary chemical behavior should be very different.

steps.text: Use the counted abundances 0.8, 0.1 and 0.1.
Mean relative atomic mass = 28.3, without units.
14 protons, 16 neutrons and 12 electrons.
Only two electrons are lost; the nucleus and isotope identity are unchanged.
Same total proton count for ten Si atoms does not fix neutron count or isotope abundances.
A larger mass can result from a greater proportion of heavier isotopes.
Neutral isotopes have the same electron configuration, so their ordinary chemistry is very similar; physical isotope effects can occur.

subject: chemistry
title: Repairing three proposed orbital diagrams
stem: The diagrams are a student’s proposed condensed configurations. The neutral atoms have Z(Cr)=24 and Z(Cu)=29; Fe has Z=26. The Fe²⁺ row shows only electrons outside [Ar]. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Correct the neutral Cr and Cu configurations, explaining the specific errors.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Correct the Fe²⁺ configuration and draw its five 3d orbital boxes.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why a box containing two upward arrows is invalid, and count the unpaired electrons in ground-state Cr and Fe²⁺.

steps.text: Cr is [Ar]3d⁵4s¹ and Cu is [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹.
The proposed 4s²3d⁴ and 4s²3d⁹ arrangements ignore the ground-state exceptions.
The corrected d counts correspond to half-filled d⁵ and filled d¹⁰ sublevels; retain the total electron counts.
Neutral Fe is [Ar]3d⁶4s²; remove the two 4s electrons first.
Fe²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁶: one paired 3d box and four singly occupied boxes with parallel unpaired spins.
Two electrons in the same orbital must have opposite spins: Pauli exclusion principle.
Cr has 6 unpaired electrons, including 4s¹; Fe²⁺ has 4.
Hund’s rule places electrons singly in degenerate d orbitals before pairing.

subject: chemistry
subtopic: Counting particles by mass: The mole
title: Combustion traps reveal an oxygen-containing formula
stem: A 0.900 g compound contains only C, H and O. Complete combustion produces 1.320 g CO₂ and 0.540 g H₂O. Its independently measured molar mass is 90.0 g mol⁻¹. Use C=12.0, H=1.0 and O=16.0. The traps separately collect all CO₂ and all H₂O. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the amounts of C and H atoms in the sample and the mass of O originally present.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine the empirical and molecular formulas.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why counting every O atom in the CO₂ and H₂O as originally belonging to the sample would be incorrect.

steps.text: Masses C=0.360 g and H=0.0600 g.
Empirical formula CH₂O; empirical formula mass 30.0.
90.0/30.0=3, so molecular formula C₃H₆O₃.
Combustion uses external O₂ as well as oxygen originally in the compound.
Product oxygen therefore cannot distinguish those two sources; oxygen by difference uses the stated C/H/O-only composition.

title: Which energy-level arrows can give an emission line?
stem: The diagram shows schematic hydrogen energy levels. A is n=3→2, B is n=4→2 and C is n=4→1. The positions illustrate relative ordering and convergence; do not measure energy differences from the page. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Rank the emitted photon energies and the wavelengths for A, B and C, explaining both orders.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why a line spectrum, rather than a continuous band of emitted energies, supports this model.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: An electron starts in n=4 and ends in n=1. State the greatest and least numbers of photons that one electron can emit in a downward-only cascade through these levels, and explain why the original arrows do not show absorption.

steps.text: B falls farther than A to the same final level; C ends at the lower n=1 level.
Energy C>B>A; wavelength A>B>C.
A larger energy gap corresponds qualitatively to higher frequency and shorter wavelength.
Only particular electron energy levels are available.
Transitions therefore have particular differences and emit discrete photon energies.
Greatest 3: 4→3→2→1; least 1: 4→1.
Emission is a downward transition to lower electron energy.
Absorption would require an upward transition and incoming energy.

title: Using orbital occupancy to distinguish an atom and its ion
stem: The diagram shows all occupied orbitals outside a [Ne] core for a neutral atom X. Each upward arrow represents one electron and empty boxes are genuinely empty. A student claims X is sulfur because three p boxes are drawn. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify X and write its full electron configuration.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Give the electron configuration of X⁴⁺ and the number of electrons removed from each occupied outer sublevel.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A proposed ground-state alternative puts both 3p electrons in the first p box. Explain its defect and distinguish an orbital from a classical electron path.

steps.text: There are 2 electrons in 3s and 2 in 3p, in addition to 10 core electrons.
Z=14: silicon; 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p².
The number of available boxes is not the number of electrons; three p orbitals exist even if some are empty.
X⁴⁺ has configuration 1s²2s²2p⁶.
Remove two 3p and two 3s electrons.
Hund’s rule requires single occupation of degenerate p orbitals before pairing.
An orbital is a region described by a high probability of finding an electron.
It is not a fixed classical trajectory around the nucleus.

title: An average formula can hide a mixture of oxides

An aggregate ratio for a mixture need not be the formula of a single chemical species.
b=0.0100 mol and a=0.0200 mol.

title: Testing the limits of the ideal-gas particle model
stem: For equal amounts of gases A and B at the same temperature, the graph shows measured pV against pressure. The horizontal reference is the ideal value nRT. Gas B initially lies below this reference, then rises above it at high pressure. No mathematical real-gas equation is needed. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State two ideal-gas particle assumptions and explain the initial downward deviation of B.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why B can lie above the ideal reference at sufficiently high pressure and predict the effect of raising temperature and lowering pressure.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A low-pressure reading gives pV=249.3 J at 300 K. Find n using the ideal approximation and explain why applying the same inference to a strongly deviating point can bias the result.

steps.text: Particles have negligible volume, and intermolecular attractions are negligible.
Attractive forces reduce the force transferred to the vessel walls relative to the ideal model.
This can make measured p, and therefore pV, lower than nRT under these conditions.
At high compression, finite particle volume is no longer negligible.
The accessible space for motion is less than the container volume, contributing to positive deviation.
Higher T and lower p generally reduce relative effects of attractions and particle volume, improving ideal behavior.
At a deviating point pV is not nRT, so dividing measured pV by RT gives an apparent amount rather than the true amount.

title: An isotope spectrum and a non-integer neutron average
stem: The mass spectrum is for singly charged iron atoms, Z=26. Peaks at m/z 54, 56, 57, 58 have relative intensities 5, 90, 3, 2. Treat each isotope mass as its integer mass number. Use Nₐ=6.02×10²³ mol⁻¹. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: b

parts.label: c

steps.text: Normalize by total intensity 100.
Abundances are 5%, 90%, 3%, 2% respectively.

subject: chemistry
title: Enriching an element starting from a measured spectrum
stem: A bromine sample gives singly charged atomic peaks at m/z 79 and 81 with relative intensities100 and 98. A 0.0100 mol portion of its atoms is mixed with pure isotope 81 until isotope 81 is70.0% of the final atoms. Treat isotope masses as integers. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the initial isotope 81 fraction and mean relative atomic mass.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the amount of pure isotope 81 added.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the mass added and the final relative atomic mass. Explain why averaging the two sample masses arithmetically would be invalid.

steps.text: The relative intensities sum to 198, not200.
Initial isotope 81 fraction=98/198=0.494949…; mean mass=79+2(98/198)=79.9899….
x=0.00684 mol to 3 significant figures.
Added mass=81x=0.554 g to 3 significant figures.

title: Two charge states do not imply six isotopes

subject: chemistry
title: Resolving an overlapping elemental isotope peak
stem: A mixture contains elements X and Y. X has only isotopes63 and 65 in atom ratio3: 1. Y has only isotopes64 and 65 in ratio1: 1. The combined singly charged atomic-ion spectrum has intensities60, 20, 40 at m/z63, 64, 65. Assume equal response per atomic ion for both elements and no fractionation. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Separate the contributions to the overlapping m/z65 peak.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the atom fraction of each element and each element’s relative atomic mass.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the mixture’s mean mass per atom and explain why the intensity at 65 cannot all be assigned to X.

steps.text: The X peak at 63 is60, so its 65 contribution is60/3=20.
The remaining 65 intensity is20 from Y, consistent with its 64 intensity 20.
X total intensity=80; Y total=40; overall=120.
Atom fractions X=2/3 and Y=1/3.
Mean masses X=63.5 and Y=64.5.
Mean mass=63.8333… relative units.
That assignment would violate both reference isotope ratios and leave Y’s64 atoms without their required65 partners.

subject: chemistry
title: Can two isotope batches produce the claimed blend?
stem: Sample A has the singly charged atomic spectrum shown: isotope 35 intensity 80 and isotope 37 intensity 20. Sample B has equal numbers of these two isotopes. A supplier claims a blend containing only A and B has mean relative atomic mass36.2. Use integer isotope masses. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the relative atomic masses of A and B.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Assess the claimed blend using isotope conservation rather than an unweighted average.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Pure isotope 37 is instead added to 1.00 mol of B atoms. Find the amount required to reach mean 36.2 and the fraction of final atoms that were added.

steps.text: Normalize A to isotope 37 fraction0.20; B has fraction0.50.
A has mean 35.4; B has mean 36.0.
Mean36.2 requires isotope 37 atom fraction(36.2−35)/2=0.60.
A/B blending can only give an isotope 37 fraction between 0.20 and 0.50.
The claim is impossible for a blend made only from A and B.
Added fraction=0.250/1.250=0.200.

title: Selective isotope removal changes both amount and mean mass
stem: The spectrum of a copper sample has atomic peaks of masses62.93 and 64.93 with relative intensities69 and 31. A 0.200 mol portion is processed so that only atoms of mass62.93 are removed, until the two remaining isotope peaks have equal intensities. Assume no response bias. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the amount and mass removed.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the remaining total amount and its mean molar mass; show a mass-conservation check.

steps.text: Use fractions0.69 and 0.31.
Mean mass63.55; isotope amounts0.138 and 0.0620 mol respectively.
The heavier isotope remains0.0620 mol, so the light isotope must also finish at 0.0620 mol.
Mass removed=0.0760×62.93=4.78 g to 3 significant figures.
Remaining amount 0.124 mol; mean molar mass(62.93+64.93)/2=63.93 g mol⁻¹.
Removed4.78268 g + remaining 0.124×63.93=7.92732 g gives12.710 g.

subject: chemistry
title: Convergence frequency fixes a molar ionization energy
stem: An emission series of neutral gaseous X atoms ends at the ground level and converges at frequency4.50×10¹⁵ Hz. Use h=6.63×10⁻³⁴ J s, c=3.00×10⁸ m s⁻¹ and Nₐ=6.02×10²³ mol⁻¹. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain why the convergence limit, rather than an arbitrary bright line, determines first ionization energy.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the convergence wavelength and first ionization energy.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Write the first-ionization equation with states and assess whether one photon of frequency4.00×10¹⁵ Hz can ionize a ground-state X atom.

steps.text: Higher bound levels approach the unbound-electron limit.
Because these transitions end at the ground level, the limiting gap is from ground-state neutral X to X⁺ plus a free electron.
A bright individual line has a smaller bound-to-bound gap; intensity does not determine threshold energy.
λ=66.7 nm to 3 significant figures.
IE=hfNₐ/1000.
IE=1.8e+03 kJ mol⁻¹.
It cannot: its photon energy is smaller than the ground-state convergence threshold, although it may match a bound excitation.

subject: chemistry
title: Different spectral limits and the cost of ionizing a sample
stem: Ground-state emission series of gaseous atoms X and Y converge at 150 nm and 300 nm respectively. A lamp transfers only 25.0% of its supplied energy into the required X-ionizing photons. Find ideal minimum energies, assuming one threshold photon per ionization. Use h=6.63×10⁻³⁴, c=3.00×10⁸, Nₐ=6.02×10²³ in SI units. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Compare and calculate the first ionization energies.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the absorbed energy needed to ionize0.0150 mol of ground-state X atoms.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the minimum supplied lamp energy and explain why a real experiment may require more.

steps.text: Shorter convergence wavelength means higher photon energy.
IE=hcNₐ/(1000λ), with λ in metres.
X: 798 and Y: 399 kJ mol⁻¹; X is exactly twiceY under the given data.
Multiply molar IE by the amount, not by an additional Avogadro factor.
Absorbed minimum=12 kJ.
Supplied energy=absorbed energy/0.250.
Minimum supplied=47.9 kJ.
The calculation assumes threshold-energy photons and one successful ionization for every photon in the stated useful fraction; other losses or unsuccessful interactions increase the demand.

subject: chemistry
title: A convergence limit from an excited level is not the first IE
stem: Two hydrogen series converge at 91.2 nm and 364.8 nm. Their lower levels are n=1 and n=2 respectively. Use h=6.63×10⁻³⁴, c=3.00×10⁸, Nₐ=6.02×10²³ in SI units. Set the energy of a free electron plus H⁺ to zero. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the limit giving first ionization energy and calculate it.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the molar energies of levels n=1 and n=2 relative to zero and the energy of emission2→1.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the wavelength of that line and explain the fourfold relation between the two ionization thresholds.

steps.text: First IE removes the electron from ground level n=1, so use91.2 nm.
IE=hcNₐ/(1000λ).
First IE=1.31e+03 kJ mol⁻¹.
Emitted energy=E₂−E₁, a positive quantity.
Photon energy for 2→1=985 kJ mol⁻¹.
Use hc/λ₂₁ = hc/91.2 nm − hc/364.8 nm.
λ₂₁=121.6 nm.
Ionization from n=2 needs one quarter of the ground-state energy because its convergence wavelength is four times as long; this does not make it the first IE.

title: Extrapolating a convergence frequency from a transformed plot
stem: A ground-state atomic emission series obeys the supplied relation f=K(1−1/n²), where n labels an excited bound level. The graph of f against1/n² is linear. The line passes through(0.25, 2.475×10¹⁵ Hz) and(0.0400, 3.168×10¹⁵ Hz). Use h=6.63×10⁻³⁴, c=3.00×10⁸, Nₐ=6.02×10²³ in SI units. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the gradient and convergence frequency from the line.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find first ionization energy and convergence wavelength.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why n→∞ corresponds to the intercept and why the individual line frequencies remain below it.

steps.text: Gradient=−3.30×10¹⁵ Hz.
The intercept at 1/n²=0 is K=3.30×10¹⁵ Hz.
IE=hKNₐ/1000 andλ=c/K.
IE=1.32×10³ kJ mol⁻¹; λ=90.9 nm to 3 significant figures.
As n increases, 1/n² approaches zero, so f approachesK.
Every finite n has1/n²>0 and f<K.
The levels converge toward the ionization limit; each finite line is a transition from a bound state, not from the free-electron limit.

subject: chemistry
title: Selective photoionization in a one-photon regime
stem: Ground-state ionization thresholds correspond to 250 nm for X atoms and 180 nm for Y atoms. A mixture is exposed to 200 nm photons. Each absorption involves one atom and one photon; simultaneous multiple-photon processes are excluded. Use h=6.63×10⁻³⁴, c=3.00×10⁸, Nₐ=6.02×10²³ in SI units. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify which element can be ionized and explain the wavelength comparison.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the200 nm photon energy and the molar thresholds for X and Y.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the energy per mole of 200 nm photons above X’s threshold and explain why merely increasing the intensity of 600 nm light cannot cross that threshold under these assumptions.

steps.text: A photon must have wavelength no longer than the threshold to supply sufficient energy.
200 nm can ionizeX, but cannot ionizeY.
Its energy exceeds the250 nm threshold but is below the180 nm threshold.
Use E=hc/λ and multiply threshold photon energies by Nₐ/1000.
200 nm photon energy=9.945×10⁻¹⁹ J.
X threshold=479; Y threshold=665 kJ mol⁻¹.
Subtract the X threshold from the molar 200 nm photon energy.
Excess=120 kJ per mole of photons.
Greater intensity supplies more600 nm photons, but each remains below the required single-photon energy; the excluded multiple-photon process cannot be assumed.

title: A wavelength calibration correction has an inverse energy effect
stem: A ground-state series-limit wavelength was reported as 200.0 nm. A calibration check establishes the true value is196.0 nm. Use h=6.63×10⁻³⁴, c=3.00×10⁸, Nₐ=6.02×10²³ in SI units. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the reported and corrected first ionization energies.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the percentage correction relative to the reported IE, then the original percentage error relative to the true IE.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why subtracting2.00% from the reported IE is wrong in both direction and exact size.

steps.text: IE=hcNₐ/(1000λ), converting nm to m.
Reported=598.689; corrected=610.907 kJ mol⁻¹.
The shorter true wavelength implies the larger IE.
Correction/report =200/196−1; original deficit/true =1−196/200.
Increase reported IE by 2.04%; original IE was2.00% low.
IE is inversely proportional to wavelength, so reducing wavelength increases IE.
The two percentages use different reference denominators.
The exact corrected/report factor is200/196, not0.98 or 1.02; the latter is only a small-error approximation.

subject: chemistry
title: A bright visible line cannot replace a convergence limit
stem: A neutral gaseous atom has a bright emission line at 650 nm. Its series ending at the ground level converges at 80.0 nm. A student uses the bright line to report first ionization energy. Use h=6.63×10⁻³⁴, c=3.00×10⁸, Nₐ=6.02×10²³ in SI units. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the student’s value and the correct first IE.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain what the bright line actually represents and why its brightness gives no direct threshold energy.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the ideal energy needed to ionize0.0100 mol of these atoms and state the state symbols required in the ionization equation.

steps.text: Calculate both hcNₐ/(1000λ) values.
Bright-line energy=184; correct first IE=1.5e+03 kJ mol⁻¹.
The correct first IE is650/80.0=8.125 times the bright-line energy.
It represents a particular difference between two bound electron levels.
Brightness concerns the number/probability of photon-producing transitions, not the energy of each photon.
Ground-state ionization requires the full gap to an unbound electron, measured by the appropriate convergence limit.
Multiply the correct molar IE by 0.0100 mol.

title: Two exceptions within an increasing first-ionization trend
stem: The graph gives first ionization energies in kJ mol⁻¹ for Na, Mg, Al, Si, P, S, Cl, Ar: 496, 738, 578, 787, 1012, 999, 1251, 1521. The atoms are gaseous and in their ground states. Use h=6.63×10⁻³⁴, c=3.00×10⁸, Nₐ=6.02×10²³ in SI units. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.prompt: Explain the overall rise from Na to Ar and the drop from Mg to Al using sublevels.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the P→S drop using orbital occupancy, rather than only saying “half-filled is stable”.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the ground-state convergence frequency and wavelength corresponding to Ar’s first IE.

steps.text: Nuclear charge increases across the same main shell, with broadly similar shielding.
Al loses a3p electron, which is higher in energy and less strongly held than Mg’s3s electron.
This sublevel change explains the local drop without reversing the overall increasing effective attraction.
P has3p³, with three singly occupied p orbitals; S has3p⁴, with one paired orbital.
Repulsion between paired electrons makes removal from S somewhat easier despite its higher nuclear charge.
Use f=1521×10³/(hNₐ), thenλ=c/f.
The appropriate series must terminate at the neutral-atom ground level; a different lower level would not measure first IE.

title: Why more protons down a group can still mean easier ionization
stem: First ionization energies of Li, Na, K are520, 496, 419 kJ mol⁻¹. Their outer occupied main levels are n=2, 3, 4 respectively. The graph supplies both trends. Use h=6.63×10⁻³⁴, c=3.00×10⁸, Nₐ=6.02×10²³ in SI units. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the convergence wavelengths for Na and K and explain their order.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A student applies K’s first IE to remove an electron from K⁺. Explain why the species and energy are wrong.

steps.text: The outer electron occupies a higher main level farther from the nucleus.
Additional inner electrons increase shielding.
These effects outweigh the increased nuclear charge for the outer electron, reducing first IE.
Use λ=hcNₐ/(1000IE).
Na: 241 nm; K: 286 nm.
K has the lower threshold energy and therefore the longer convergence wavelength.
First IE is K(g) → K⁺(g)+e⁻; the next step is K⁺(g) → K²⁺(g)+e⁻.
K⁺ has already lost its 4s electron; a further electron is removed from a lower core level and is much more strongly held.

title: The energetic cost of removing a core electron
stem: An element X in period 3 has successive ionization energies496, 4562, 6910, 9543 kJ mol⁻¹, shown on a logarithmic vertical scale. Use Nₐ=6.02×10²³ mol⁻¹. The atom loses one electron in each step. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the energy needed to convert0.0200 mol of X(g) entirely to X³⁺(g).

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Compare this with forming X⁺ and explain why the energy pattern supports X⁺ as the common ionic charge without claiming X³⁺ cannot exist at all.

steps.text: The largest jump is between the first and second ionizations, so there is one outer-shell electron.
Group1; X isNa, with 1s²2s²2p⁶3s¹.
The second electron is removed from the completed inner shell.
Each atom must undergo all three steps; total per mole=496+4562+6910.
Total=11968 kJ mol⁻¹; sample energy=239 kJ to 3 significant figures.
Formation of 0.0200 mol X⁺ needs9.92 kJ.
Further removal is much more costly because it starts removing core electrons.
The data support the favored simple ion but do not forbid a higher gaseous charge state if sufficient energy is supplied.

title: Electron capture reverses a specified ionization step
stem: Magnesium has IE₁=738 and IE₂=1451 kJ mol⁻¹. Consider gaseous Mg, Mg⁺ and Mg²⁺ with free electrons available. The diagram shows the sequence, without assigning an energy zero. Use h=6.63×10⁻³⁴, c=3.00×10⁸, Nₐ=6.02×10²³ in SI units. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Give the energy change for Mg²⁺(g)+e⁻→Mg⁺(g), and for Mg⁺(g)+e⁻→Mg(g). Explain the signs.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the total energy released when0.0100 mol Mg²⁺ captures enough electrons to become neutral, and count the captured electrons.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the ground-state convergence wavelength for the reverse first-ionization step and explain why it is not the threshold for Mg⁺ ionization.

steps.text: The changes are−1451 and−738 kJ mol⁻¹ respectively.
Each capture exactly reverses the corresponding endothermic ionization step.
The second IE must be paired with Mg⁺→Mg²⁺, not with neutral Mg→Mg⁺.
Two captures per atom release(1451+738)×0.0100.
21.9 kJ released; system energy change−21.9 kJ to 3 significant figures.
0.0200 mol electrons=1.20×10²² electrons.
λ=162 nm; Mg⁺ ionization instead requires IE₂=1451 kJ mol⁻¹.

title: Two ionization patterns predict an ionic composition
stem: Two period 3 elements X and Y have the successive ionization data shown. X: 580, 1817, 2744, 11577 kJ mol⁻¹. Y: 1000, 2250, 3360, 4560, 7010, 8500, 27107 kJ mol⁻¹. Assume the usual simple ions that achieve noble-gas configurations. Use Nₐ=6.02×10²³ mol⁻¹. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a

title: A spectrum measured from cations determines a second IE
stem: A series recorded from gaseous Mg⁺ ions terminates at the ground level of Mg⁺ and converges at 3.63544×10¹⁵ Hz. Neutral Mg has first IE 738 kJ mol⁻¹. Use h=6.63×10⁻³⁴, c=3.00×10⁸, Nₐ=6.02×10²³ in SI units. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write the ionization represented by this limit and explain why its energy is not Mg’s first IE.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the energy represented by the limit and the total energy per mole for Mg(g)→Mg²⁺(g)+2e⁻.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the energy for 0.0400 mol of initially neutral Mg to become Mg²⁺ and compare the Mg⁺ and neutral Mg electron configurations.

steps.text: Mg⁺(g) → Mg²⁺(g)+e⁻.
The starting species is a singly charged ion, so the limit measures removal of its next electron.
It is the second IE relative to neutral Mg’s successive-ionization sequence.
IE₂=hfNₐ/1000≈1451 kJ mol⁻¹.
Total=738+1451≈2189 kJ mol⁻¹.
Use 0.0400 times the sum of both ionization energies.
87.6 kJ to 3 significant figures.
Mg: [Ne]3s²; Mg⁺: [Ne]3s¹. Both removed electrons originate in 3s, but the second is held more strongly by the positive ion.

title: A logarithmic IE plot and the cost of one additional removal
stem: A period 3 element has successive ionization energies1012, 1907, 2914, 4963, 6274, 21267 kJ mol⁻¹, plotted on a logarithmic scale. Each step removes one electron from the preceding gaseous species. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the element and explain where its valence-to-core boundary occurs.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Compare the energy to remove the first five electrons with that for removing only the sixth, per mole of atoms.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the total energy to convert0.0100 mol atoms to 6+ ions and explain why equal vertical gaps on the logarithmic plot do not mean equal energy differences.

steps.text: The marked jump is after the fifth removed electron.
Five valence electrons imply group 15; the period 3 element is phosphorus.
Its ground configuration is[Ne]3s²3p³; removal6 begins from the lower[Ne]core.
Sum IE₁ through IE₅.
First five sum17070 kJ mol⁻¹; sixth alone21267 kJ mol⁻¹.
A single core electron therefore costs more to remove than all five valence electrons combined.
Total per mole=17070+21267=38337 kJ mol⁻¹.
Sample energy 383 kJ to 3 significant figures.
Equal log-axis separations represent equal ratios, not equal additive IE differences.

title: Charge carriers change when an ionic material melts
stem: A dry binary material contains ions M²⁺ and X⁻. The graph shows current at equal voltages for its solid and molten states. The melt conducts, while the intact solid does not. Decomposition and chemical reactions at the electrodes are excluded from this comparison. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Deduce the empirical formula and describe the solid’s bonding model.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the change in conductivity on melting and identify the moving charge carriers.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A student claims melting must turn MX₂ into neutral M and X₂. Evaluate that claim using the observations and atom/charge accounting.

steps.text: Neutrality requires two X⁻ ions per M²⁺.
Formula MX₂.
A giant ionic lattice contains oppositely charged ions held by electrostatic attractions in all directions.
In the solid the ions occupy fixed lattice positions and cannot migrate through the material.
Melting allows ions to move under the applied field.
Both cations and anions carry charge; the explanation does not require free electrons as in a metal.
Melting is a physical loss of lattice order and does not itself discharge the ions.
Neutral M and X₂ would require electron transfer, not just ion movement.
The conductivity evidence is consistent with mobile M²⁺ and X⁻, not proof of formation of neutral elements.

title: Inferring an ionic formula and lattice-strength comparison
stem: Ion A contains12 protons and 10 electrons; ion B contains8 protons and 10 electrons. A schematic lattice slice is shown. Ionic radii are A: 72 pm, B: 140 pm, Na⁺: 102 pm, Cl⁻: 181 pm. Compare attraction qualitatively; no lattice-enthalpy calculation is required. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the ions, their charges and the neutral formula.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Predict whether MgO or NaCl should have stronger electrostatic lattice attractions, using both charge and size.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why ions being isoelectronic does not make them identical particles or force equal ionic radii.

steps.text: Charge is proton count minus electron count.
A isMg²⁺ and B isO²⁻; formula MgO.
Each ion has10 electrons, a neon-like electron configuration.
Mg²⁺/O²⁻ have larger charge magnitudes than Na⁺/Cl⁻.
The supplied Mg²⁺/O²⁻ radii also give a smaller interionic separation.
Both factors support stronger attractions in MgO and a generally higher melting temperature.
Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ have different nuclear proton numbers, 12 and 8.
With the same electron count, the greater nuclear attraction in Mg²⁺ draws its electron cloud in more strongly.

subject: chemistry
title: Why a shifted ionic layer fractures rather than flows
stem: The diagram is a schematic ionic lattice slice after its lower rows have shifted relative to the upper rows. Compare it with a metal whose positive cores remain immersed in delocalized electrons when rows shift. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain the mechanical consequence of the ionic layer shift.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why the corresponding shift is compatible with metallic malleability.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Compare electrical conductivity of the intact ionic solid and the metal, naming carriers in each.

steps.text: The shift brings some like-charged ions into closer opposition.
Repulsion between like charges can split the crystal.
The ionic solid is brittle rather than generally malleable.
Metallic attraction is between positive cores and a shared delocalized electron population.
It is not a set of directional localized bonds that must all break on sliding.
The electron population can continue attracting the shifted cores.
The metal conducts through mobile delocalized electrons.
In the ionic solid the ions are fixed; neither a mobile ion population nor metallic delocalized electrons is available.

title: Dilution changes ion concentration without destroying ions
stem: 0.0100 mol Na₂SO₄ dissolves completely in 100.0 cm³ water, giving a final solution volume treated as 100.0 cm³. At fixed voltage and temperature, assume current is proportional to the total concentration of mobile ions. The graph shows current on subsequent dilution. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the initial amounts and concentrations of the two ions.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: The volume is doubled to 200.0 cm³. Predict the current ratio and state what happens to the total number of ions.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why this result does not show that all ionic solids are soluble in water, or that the ions have lost their charges.

steps.text: Na₂SO₄ gives2Na⁺ and 1SO₄²⁻ per formula unit.
Amounts: Na⁺ 0.0200 mol, SO₄²⁻ 0.0100 mol.
Concentrations: Na⁺ 0.200 and SO₄²⁻ 0.100 mol dm⁻³.
All ion concentrations halve at fixed amount.
New/old current=1/2; total number of ions is unchanged.
The question states complete dissolution for this particular salt; solubility depends on the competing interactions for each material.
Dilution separates ions more widely but does not supply electrons to neutralize them.
The solution remains electrically neutral overall because2Na⁺ balances oneSO₄²⁻.

subject: chemistry
title: The same electron-domain count gives three different shapes
stem: The drawing gives bond connectivity only, not spatial geometry, for CH₄, NH₃ and H₂O. Complete the Lewis models and use them to evaluate the claim that all three must have the same molecular shape. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Count the valence electrons and central lone pairs in each.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: State the electron-domain geometry and molecular shape for each.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Predict the bond-angle order and explain why identical total valence-electron counts are not enough to predict identical shape.

steps.text: Total valence counts are8 for CH₄, 8 for NH₃ and 8 for H₂O.
Central lone pairs are0, 1, 2 respectively.
All three have four central electron domains, counting each bond as one domain.
All have tetrahedral electron-domain geometry.
Molecular shapes: CH₄ tetrahedral, NH₃ trigonal pyramidal, H₂O bent.
Molecular shape describes atom positions; lone-pair domains are omitted from the shape name.
H–C–H > H–N–H > H–O–H, approximately109.5°, 107°, 104.5°.
Lone-pair repulsions compress bonding domains; their differing number matters even though all totals are8 electrons.

subject: chemistry
title: Two three-atom molecules have different dipole cancellation
stem: Compare CO₂ and OF₂ using the connectivity frameworks shown; they are not spatial drawings. Electronegativity values: C2.55, O3.44, F3.98. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Complete their Lewis formulas, including all lone pairs, and count valence electrons.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Deduce their molecular geometries and polarities.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Identify the negative end of each bond and explain why the central O in OF₂ need not be its negative end.

steps.text: CO₂ has16 valence electrons; OF₂ has20.
CO₂: O=C=O, each O has2 lone pairs; central C has none.
OF₂: twoO–F single bonds; central O has2 lone pairs and each F has3.
CO₂ is linear and nonpolar; OF₂ is bent and polar.
The twoC=O bond dipoles cancel in linearCO₂.
The O–F bond dipoles do not cancel in bentOF₂.
C=O is negative towardO; O–F is negative towardF.
F is more electronegative than O; bond polarity depends on the bonded pair, not on a universal assignment thatO is always negative.

title: A donor–acceptor adduct changes the boron geometry
stem: NH₃ and BF₃ react to form the adduct H₃N→BF₃. The arrow shows the newly formed bond, not a reaction mechanism. Use the initial connectivity models to identify the electron source. Atomic valence counts: H=1, N=5, B3, F=7. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.prompt: Identify the donor, acceptor and origin of the new bonding pair.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Deduce the change in boron electron-domain and molecular geometry.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Count the total valence electrons before and after adduct formation, and explain whether the new bond remains a uniquely weaker “one-electron bond”.

steps.text: NH₃ donates its nitrogen lone pair; BF₃ accepts it at boron.
Both electrons in the new coordination bond originate from N.
BF₃ is electron-deficient before bonding, with only six electrons around B.
BF₃ has three domains and trigonal-planar geometry at B.
In the adductB has four bonding domains and tetrahedral geometry.
BF₃ has24 and NH₃ has8 valence electrons.
The adduct has32; no electron is created or lost.
It is a shared two-electron covalent bond; “coordination” describes the pair’s origin, not a one-electron bond or an automatic statement of lower strength.

subject: chemistry
title: An ether can accept water hydrogen bonds without self-donating
stem: The structures are ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH, and dimethyl ether, CH₃OCH₃. Both have molar mass46.0 g mol⁻¹. Their boiling points are78 °C and−24 °C respectively. Consider ordinary intermolecular forces, not chemical reaction. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain the boiling-point difference using structural features rather than molar mass alone.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how ether can nevertheless hydrogen-bond to water. Identify the donor and acceptor atoms.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Predict the more volatile pure substance and compare electrical conductivity of their pure liquids, explaining the charge carriers.

steps.text: Both have London forces and polar bonds.
Ethanol molecules can formO–H···O hydrogen bonds with each other.
Dimethyl ether has an O lone pair but noO–H bond, so pure ether cannot form the corresponding self-donated hydrogen-bond network.
A waterO–H group donates a hydrogen bond to an etherO lone pair.
The ether is an acceptor; it does not need anO–H bond to accept a hydrogen bond.
Dimethyl ether is more volatile, consistent with its much lower boiling point.
Neither neutral molecular liquid provides a substantial mobile-ion population or metallic delocalized electrons.
Hydrogen bonding is an intermolecular attraction, not production of freely moving charged ions.

title: Polarity does not by itself rank every boiling point
stem: Compare CCl₄ and CH₂Cl₂. Connectivity is shown, not spatial geometry. Both central carbon atoms have four single bonds and no lone pairs. Their boiling points are77 °C and 40 °C respectively. Electronegativity: C2.55, Cl 3.16, H2.20. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Deduce the molecular geometry and polarity of each.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why the higher boiling point of nonpolarCCl₄ does not contradict the role of dipole–dipole forces.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A student draws the central carbon as square-planar to make oppositeC–Cl bonds cancel. Explain why that argument is invalid.

steps.text: Both are tetrahedral around C.
CCl₄’s four equalC–Cl dipoles cancel by symmetry, so it is nonpolar.
CH₂Cl₂ is polar because its differing bond dipoles cannot all cancel.
CCl₄ has a larger electron cloud and more electrons than CH₂Cl₂.
Its stronger London dispersion forces can outweigh the extra dipole–dipole attraction in CH₂Cl₂.
Intermolecular-force ranking must compare the whole structures; comparable molar mass was not stipulated here.
Four domains around an ordinary carbon center give tetrahedral rather than square-planar VSEPR geometry.
A desired polarity outcome cannot justify replacing the chemically appropriate spatial model.

title: Two carbon networks can have different electrical behavior
stem: The figures show local connectivity for two carbon allotropes. A is a three-connected planar sheet; B is a four-connected three-dimensional network. All dangling fragment edges continue into the bulk material. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain whyA can conduct along its sheet whereas ideal pure B is an electrical insulator.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why both are described as network covalent solids and why graphite can still be softer than diamond.

steps.text: A: graphene, or one layer of graphite; B: diamond.
A has approximately120° planar local bonding; B has approximately109.5° tetrahedral local bonding.
InA, one valence electron per carbon participates in a delocalized electron population along the sheet.
InB, all four valence electrons are involved in localized covalent bonding.
B has no comparable mobile delocalized population; atomic connectivity affects carrier availability.
Strong covalent bonds extend through the relevant network rather than forming small independent molecules.
Diamond is a continuous rigid three-dimensional network.
In graphite, weak attractions between covalently bonded sheets permit sliding; this does not mean the bonds inside each sheet are weak.

subject: chemistry
title: A network formula must account for shared oxygen atoms
stem: The diagram illustrates a fragment of silicon dioxide. In the extended structure each Si is bonded to four O atoms and every O bridges two Si atoms. Compare this material with molecularCO₂. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Derive the bulk Si: O ratio from connectivity, explaining why simply counting the displayed fragment can mislead.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why SiO₂ has a much higher melting temperature than CO₂.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Compare the meaning of “molecule” and “formula unit” here, and explain why pure SiO₂ does not conduct like graphite.

steps.text: Four Si–O connections per Si are shared by two Si neighbors per O.
O per Si=4/2=2; formula SiO₂.
The finite cut fragment omits continuing Si atoms and cannot be treated as an isolated molecular formula.
MeltingSiO₂ substantially disrupts a covalent network with many strong bonds.
OrdinaryCO₂ melting/sublimation overcomes attractions between discrete molecules rather than breaking each C=O bond.
The sharedXO₂ formula pattern alone does not imply the same structural type.
CO₂ consists of discrete molecules; SiO₂ expresses a bulk ratio in a network, not separateSiO₂ molecules.
IdealSiO₂ has no analogous mobile delocalized-electron population or mobile ions in its solid network.

title: A matched chromatography spot is evidence, not unique identification
stem: The TLC plate uses a polar stationary phase. Solvent front displacement is8.0 cm; reference spotsA, B, C move1.6, 5.2, 6.8 cm. The unknown mixture has spots aligned with A and B. All lanes are developed together. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the three reference retardation factors and identify the most strongly retained reference.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the separation in terms of competing intermolecular attractions.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Assess the claim that the unknown is definitely a pure mixture of only A and B, and suggest a stronger check.

steps.text: R_F=distance travelled by spot/distance travelled by solvent front.
A is most strongly retained relative to this mobile phase.
A substance partitions according to relative attraction to stationary and mobile phases.
Greater relative attraction to the stationary phase slows migration.
R_F values are specific to the stated phases and conditions, not intrinsic constants for a compound.
The two spots are consistent with A and B but a different component can share anR_F or co-migrate.
Repeat with another suitable mobile/stationary phase or use an independent analytical method; agreement in one system alone is not unique proof.

title: The bonding triangle cannot distinguish every structural type
stem: Use the blank bonding triangle and these electronegativities: Na 0.93, Cl 3.16, Si 1.90, C2.55. For each binary compound use mean electronegativity horizontally and absolute difference vertically. Compare NaCl, SiCl₄ and SiC. No percentage ionic-character formula is required. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the coordinates of each compound.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Identify the strongest ionic tendency and explain why the triangle represents a continuum rather than an exact threshold rule.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: SiCl₄ is molecular whereasSiC is a covalent network. Explain why their broadly covalent positions alone do not predict their melting temperatures or imply the same structure.

steps.text: Compute the arithmetic mean and absolute difference for each bonded element pair.
NaCl has the largest electronegativity difference and strongest ionic tendency of these three.
Bond character changes continuously with electron sharing and charge separation.
A single numerical boundary is not a universal proof of completely ionic or completely covalent bonding.
The triangle addresses relative bond character rather than the full connectivity of a material.
A network requires disruption of many strong covalent bonds on melting, whereas a molecular material primarily overcomes intermolecular attractions.
Therefore connectivity and particle type are additional information needed for property predictions.

title: Nitrate bond equivalence requires more than one localized drawing
stem: One localized bonding framework for NO₃⁻ is shown. Complete all octets using N=5 and O=6 valence electrons. Experiment finds all three N–O bonds equivalent. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Count valence electrons and assign formal charges in the displayed localized form.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Draw the other resonance contributors and explain the observed equivalence.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the mean N–O bond order and predict the geometry around N.

steps.text: Total=5+3(6)+1=24 electrons.
N has formal charge+1; double-bonded O has0; each single-bonded O has−1.
The charges sum to−1, matching the ion rather than assigning its entire charge to N.
Move the double bond to either of the other O atoms, keeping the nuclear connectivity and total electron count unchanged.
The actual electron density is delocalized over the three N–O links.
The ion is not rapidly alternating between three unequal physical bond arrangements.
The total localized bond-order sum is2+1+1=4 across three equivalent links.
Mean bond order4/3; three electron domains give trigonal-planar geometry, approximately120°.

subject: chemistry
title: Ozone has equal bonds without two simultaneous double bonds
stem: Ozone has O–O distances of 128 pm, compared with 121 pm in O₂ and 148 pm for a typical O–O single bond. A localized O₃ framework is shown. Use 6 valence electrons per O. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Complete the Lewis formula and assign formal charges.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the measured bond lengths using resonance and estimate the equivalent bond order.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Predict the molecular shape and reject the proposed structure O=O=O with no central lone pair.

steps.text: O₃ has18 valence electrons; complete each octet with one single and one double bond at the central O.
Central O is+1; single-bonded terminal O is−1; double-bonded terminal O is0.
The second contributor swaps the single and double bond positions.
Delocalization makes the two actual bonds equivalent and intermediate in length.
Equivalent bond order is(1+2)/2=1.5.
Central O has three domains: two bonding domains and one lone pair; the molecule is bent.
O=O=O with no central lone pair cannot distribute18 electrons while maintaining the intended central/terminal octets and correct total count.
Resonance does not mean adding the two contributors together to give two full double bonds.

title: Amide planarity is evidence that a lone pair is delocalized
stem: Formamide H–C(=O)–NH₂ is observed to be planar around N and has a shorter C–N bond than a typical amine. The alternative resonance framework H–C(–O)=NH₂ is shown beside it. Complete octets and formal charges. Use H=1, C=4, N=5, O=6 valence electrons. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Count valence electrons and assign the formal charges introduced in the second contributor.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the N planarity and short C–N bond using orbital overlap.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Count sigma and localized pi bonds in the neutral first drawing, and explain why adding the pi bonds from both contributors would be wrong.

steps.text: Total=3+4+5+6=18 electrons.
In the second contributor, O is−1 and N is+1; C and H have0.
The total remains0; the electron pair has been redistributed without moving nuclei or transferring an electron out of the molecule.
An unhybridized p orbital at N allows its lone pair to overlap with the neighboring carbonylπ system.
An sp² model at N is consistent with the observed planar three-bond geometry.
Delocalization gives partial C–N double-bond character and contributes to restricted rotation.
First drawing: 5σ bonds and 1 localizedπ bond.
The contributors describe alternative representations of one electron distribution, not two molecules whose bond counts are added.

subject: chemistry
title: Choosing the lone-pair site in sulfur tetrafluoride
stem: For SF₄, use S=6 and F=7 valence electrons. The five-site model is supplied to compare axial and equatorial placement, not as a completed Lewis formula. Each terminal F has three lone pairs. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Count total valence electrons and deduce the central lone-pair count.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Choose the lone-pair site type using 90° contacts and predict molecular geometry.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Compare SF₄ with SF₆ in electron-domain count and molecular polarity.

steps.text: SF₄ has6+4(7)=34 electrons; F lone pairs use24 and fourS–F bonds use8.
Two electrons remain onS: one lone pair, five central domains.
An axial site has three90° contacts to equatorial domains; an equatorial site has two to axial domains.
The lone pair favors an equatorial site; molecular shape is seesaw.
Lone-pair repulsion distorts the ideal bond angles; the bonding framework is not a square-planar four-domain structure.
SF₆ has six bonding domains, no central lone pair, and octahedral geometry.
Its equalS–F dipoles cancel by symmetry, whereas SF₄’s seesaw arrangement does not cancel them.
SF₆ is nonpolar; SF₄ is polar.

title: Two lone pairs convert a five-domain framework into a T shape
stem: ClF₃ has7 valence electrons from Cl and 7 from each F. Use the five-site drawing and complete terminal-F octets. A student counts only threeCl–F bonds and proposes trigonal-planar geometry. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine the central nonbonding pairs and electron-domain geometry.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Place the lone pairs, identify the remaining bond positions, and give molecular shape and polarity.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why NF₃ cannot be assigned the same two-lone-pair model, and correct the student’s initial reasoning.

steps.text: Total28 electrons; terminal-F lone pairs use18 and three bonds use6.
Four electrons remain: two central lone pairs; five domains give trigonal-bipyramidal electron-domain geometry.
Both lone pairs favor equatorial sites to reduce90° contacts.
Two axial bonds and one equatorial bond remain, giving a T-shaped molecule.
The three bond dipoles do not cancel; ClF₃ is polar.
NF₃ has5+3(7)=26 electrons, two fewer than ClF₃.
NF₃ has one central lone pair and trigonal-pyramidal molecular geometry.
Bond count alone misses nonbonding domains; second-period N also cannot exceed its octet in a normal Lewis model.

subject: chemistry
title: Linear molecules need not have the same central-domain count
stem: Compare XeF₂ and CO₂. Xe supplies8 valence electrons, F=7, C=4 and O=6. The drawing supplies a five-site option for Xe; the CO₂ connectivity is O=C=O. Determine whether “linear” always implies two central electron domains. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Complete XeF₂ electron accounting and assign its lone-pair sites.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Compare the molecular geometries and central-domain counts of XeF₂ and CO₂.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Compare polarity and explain why an sp label should not automatically be assigned to Xe merely from the linear nuclear arrangement.

steps.text: Total22 electrons; terminal-F lone pairs use12 and two bonds use4.
Six electrons remain: threeXe lone pairs and five domains.
All three lone pairs occupy equatorial sites, leaving the two axial bonds.
Both are linear, but XeF₂ has five domains and CO₂ has two.
Multiple bonds each count as oneVSEPR domain, so CO₂’s two double bonds give two domains.
A molecular shape name counts nuclear positions and does not reveal all lone-pair domains.
Both ideal molecules have canceling equal opposite bond dipoles and are nonpolar.
The sp two-domain model fits central C in CO₂; it is not justified for Xe’s five-domain electron distribution merely by the same molecular shape.

title: Opposite lone pairs explain square-planar xenon tetrafluoride
stem: For XeF₄, use Xe=8 and F=7 valence electrons. The six-site diagram shows three pairs of opposite directions. Complete all terminal-F octets before choosing which two sites are not occupied by F. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine total electrons, the number of central lone pairs, and electron-domain geometry.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Choose the lone-pair arrangement and derive the molecular shape.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find formal charge onXe and comment on molecular polarity.

steps.text: Total36; F lone pairs use24 and fourXe–F bonds use8.
Four nonbonding electrons remain: two lone pairs; six domains give octahedral electron-domain geometry.
The two lone pairs favor opposite sites, 180° apart, rather than adjacent90° sites.
The other fourF atoms lie in a square plane; the molecule is square planar.
Any of the three equivalent opposite-site pairs can be chosen; rotating the whole model does not create a different molecular shape.
Formal charge Xe=8−4−4.
Xe formal charge 0; each F also0.
Equal bond dipoles cancel within the square, so the ideal molecule is nonpolar.

subject: chemistry
title: Five bonds do not always mean trigonal-bipyramidal molecules
stem: Iodine pentafluoride, IF₅, contains I=7 and F=7 valence electrons. A candidate six-site arrangement is shown. Compare the proposal “five bonds means five domains” with a full electron count. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine the number of central electron domains and identify the omitted feature in the proposal.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Deduce electron-domain and molecular geometry, including ideal angle families.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Assess polarity and central octet compliance.

steps.text: Total42 electrons; five terminal-F octets require30 lone-pair electrons and 10 bonding electrons.
Two electrons remain onI: one lone pair; six total domains.
The proposal omits that nonbonding domain.
Electron-domain geometry is octahedral; molecular shape is square pyramidal.
Approximate bond-angle families are90° and 180°, with lone-pair distortion possible.
The missing sixth atom is a lone-pair site, not a reason to change the six-domain framework into trigonal bipyramidal.
The one-apex square-pyramidal arrangement does not cancel all bond dipoles; IF₅ is polar.
Five bonding pairs plus one lone pair place12 valence-shell electrons around I; this is an allowed period 5 expanded-octet case, not a second-period N octet.

title: An octahedral mixed-ligand molecule can have two dipole patterns
stem: A hypothetical octahedral SF₄Cl₂ model has six central bonding domains. Opposite direction pairs are+x/−x, +y/−y, +z/−z. ModelT hasCl on+z and−z; model C hasCl on+x and+y. Every other site isF. For this comparison, each S→F bond dipole has magnitude2 units and each S→Cl dipole1 unit. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Count the total valence electrons and central lone pairs, using S=6, F=7, Cl=7.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Assess the net dipole of model T and justify the cancellation.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the vector components for model C and compare its polarity with T.

steps.text: Six bonds use12 electrons and terminal lone pairs use36, leaving no central lone pair.
The twoCl dipoles cancel alongz; each oppositeF pair also cancels.
The vector sum is zero, so model T is nonpolar within the supplied ideal model.
Alongx: +1 from Cl and−2 from F gives−1; the same holds alongy; z contributions cancel.
Net components(−1, −1, 0), magnitude√2 dipole units.
ModelC is polar; identical molecular formula and electron-domain geometry do not ensure identical ligand symmetry or polarity.
The numerical result uses the supplied dipole magnitudes and is not a claim of universal S–F/S–Cl dipole values.

subject: chemistry
title: Formal-charge preference must still respect a second-period octet
stem: For POCl₃, two proposed Lewis formulas have the same P–O/threeP–Cl connectivity: one uses P=O, the other P–O. Complete all terminal octets. Use P=5, N=5, O=6, Cl=7 valence electrons. Then consider replacing P by N in this connectivity without changing total atom counts. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find total valence electrons and formal charges in the two P-containing proposals.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Choose the preferred P formula using formal-charge criteria and state its central domain count.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why copying that double-bond arrangement onto N is invalid and give an octet-compliant charge assignment instead.

steps.text: Total=5+6+3(7)=32 electrons.
P=O form: all formal charges0; P–O form: P+1, O−1, each Cl 0.
The P=O formula minimizes charge separation and is a preferred localized Lewis representation.
P can have an expanded octet; it has10 electrons around it in that representation.
There are four central electron domains because the double bond counts as one domain.
ThreeN–Cl single bonds plusN=O would put10 electrons around second-period N, violating its octet.
Use four single bonds with N+1, O−1 and Cl 0 instead.
Formal-charge minimization cannot justify violating the second-period octet; the comparison is about Lewis models, not a claim that the hypothetical N compound is experimentally stable.

title: Transition-metal bonding is richer than a one-s-electron model
stem: The plotted melting temperatures areNa98 °C, Mg 650 °C, Cr 1907 °C, Fe1538 °C. A simplified metallic model is used, with positive atomic cores surrounded by delocalized electrons. A student claims that only outer s electrons can contribute to bonding and that melting point must rise monotonically with d-electron count. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain how transition metals can have stronger metallic bonding than a simple one-electron s-block metal.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Use the data to evaluate the monotonic-curve claim.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why a transition metal can conduct while solid and remain malleable despite strong bonding.

steps.text: Transition-metal d electrons can contribute to delocalized metallic bonding as well as s electrons.
The resulting attraction can involve a higher density of bonding electrons and positive cores.
This supports high melting temperatures without requiring discrete metal molecules.
Cr has ground-state3d⁵4s¹ and Fe has3d⁶4s², yet Cr melts above Fe despite Fe’s larger d-electron count.
d-block bonding depends on how d orbitals and electrons contribute, not on a simple count-only rule.
The simple charge/radius/electron-pool picture has limits and does not predict every d-block melting-point trend by itself.
Mobile delocalized electrons carry charge through the solid.
Non-directional metallic attraction can persist as positive cores shift relative to one another, so strong metallic bonding is compatible with malleability.

title: Deriving a polyester repeat rather than an addition-polymer repeat
stem: The monomers are HO–CH₂–CH₂–OH and HOOC–C₆H₄–COOH. The ring group C₆H₄ has its two acid substituents at opposite positions. Condensation makes ester links and eliminates water. For the ideal repeat-unit formula, neglect chain-end corrections. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Draw one constitutional repeating unit, including the connecting bonds that continue into neighboring repeats.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine the repeat-unit formula and small-molecule loss per diol/diacid pair.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why this is condensation polymerization and predict two structural reasons it may be less flexible than a simple hydrocarbon addition chain.

steps.text: Join diol O to acid carbonyl C at each new ester link.
A valid repeat is[–O–CH₂–CH₂–O–C(=O)–C₆H₄–C(=O)–]ₙ.
The bracket endpoints must continue through the ester-linked backbone, not cap the repeat with unreacted acid/diol ends.
Monomers areC₂H₆O₂ and C₈H₆O₄; subtract2H₂O in the ideal repeat.
Repeat formula C₁₀H₈O₄; two water molecules lost per ideal repeat.
Water is eliminated while ester links form; the backbone contains O rather than retaining all monomer atoms as an addition polymer does.
The aromatic ring restricts backbone flexibility.
Polar ester groups provide stronger intermolecular attractions than a comparable nonpolar hydrocarbon segment.

title: Reading the monomers back from a polyamide backbone
stem: A diamine H₂N–(CH₂)₆–NH₂ and diacid HOOC–(CH₂)₄–COOH form a polyamide. The displayed condensed structures show every functional-group connection. Neglect chain ends when writing the ideal repeating-unit formula. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Draw an appropriate repeating unit and identify the group connecting adjacent monomer residues.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the repeat-unit molecular formula and identify the bonds that would be cut to recover the monomer frameworks by hydrolysis.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why this polymer can form interchain hydrogen bonds and why those attractions must not be called the covalent backbone links.

steps.text: Form C(=O)–NH links between acid and amine ends, with water loss.
A valid repeat is[–NH–(CH₂)₆–NH–C(=O)–(CH₂)₄–C(=O)–]ₙ; connecting group is amide.
C₆H₁₆N₂+C₆H₁₀O₄−2H₂O gives the ideal repeat.
Repeat formula C₁₂H₂₂N₂O₂.
Hydrolysis cuts the amide C(=O)–N links; it does not cut arbitrary C–C bonds in the methylene chains.
N–H groups can donate hydrogen bonds and carbonylO atoms can accept them.
These attractions act between appropriate neighboring chain regions.
The chain itself is maintained by covalent amide and C–C bonds; breaking hydrogen bonds does not by itself hydrolyze the polymer.

subject: chemistry
title: Functional-group balance can create a crosslinked polyester
stem: A triol with formula C₃H₈O₃ has threeOH groups; a diacidC₄H₆O₄ has twoCOOH groups. They undergo ester-forming condensation. Consider ideal bulk functional-group stoichiometry with chain-end corrections neglected; do not interpret the bulk formula balance as one discrete molecule. Use monomer molar masses92.0 and 118.0 g mol⁻¹ and water18.0 g mol⁻¹. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the triol: diacid mole ratio needed for equal numbers of OH and COOH functions.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: For a2 mol-triol/3 mol-diacid stoichiometric feed, find the maximum water produced and polymer mass retained under the stated idealization.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why this feed can produce a branched/crosslinked material rather than the strictly linear structure from a diol, and predict an effect on flow when heated.

steps.text: If amounts aret and a, matching functions gives3t=2a.
Triol: diacid=2: 3.
There are sixOH and sixCOOH functions, allowing six ester-forming condensations.
Maximum water=6 mol=108 g.
Feed mass=2(92.0)+3(118.0)=538 g; retained polymer mass=430 g.
A triol can connect in three directions rather than only two.
Interconnected covalent junctions can prevent entire chains from sliding independently.
A strongly crosslinked network will resist ordinary melt flow; heating that destroys the network would involve bond breaking rather than merely overcoming intermolecular attractions.
